body.p: A pointer is a variable that holds the address of another object: a variable, an array, an array element, a constant, or a pseudo-variable. Pointers are new in JALv3 and are supported on every target. Every pointer declaration names the type of the object it may point at, the pointee contract.

section.title: Declaring a pointer
section.p: The preferred form puts the pointee contract after AS:
section.codeblock: VAR POINTER p AS VAR BYTE -- points at a writable byte VAR POINTER cp AS CONST BYTE -- points at a read-only byte VAR POINTER ap AS VAR BYTE[5] -- points at one five-byte array VAR POINTER slots[3] AS VAR BYTE -- three pointer slots
section.p: The older spellings are also accepted:
section.codeblock: VAR POINTER VAR BYTE p VAR POINTER CONST BYTE cp VAR POINTER p(AS VAR BYTE)
section.p: A pointer occupies 2 bytes on the classic PIC cores, 3 bytes on PIC18, and 4 bytes on PIC32 and ESP32.

section.title: Binding a pointer
section.p: The IS statement makes a pointer refer to an object. It does not copy a value; it binds the address:
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE value = 10 VAR POINTER p AS VAR BYTE
p IS value -- p now points at value
section.p: The target may be a variable, an array, an array element, a constant array, a compatible pseudo-variable, or another pointer:
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE arr[4] VAR POINTER whole AS VAR BYTE[4] VAR POINTER element AS VAR BYTE VAR POINTER other AS VAR BYTE
whole IS arr -- the array element IS arr[2] -- one element other IS whole -- copy the pointer value (not the pointee)
section.p: Binding a pointer array element works with a constant or a runtime index: slots[k] IS value.

section.title: Reading and writing through a pointer
section.p: Using a pointer as a value reads the pointee; assigning to it writes the pointee. Both require the pointer to have been bound.
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE value = 10 VAR BYTE copy VAR POINTER p AS VAR BYTE
p IS value copy = p -- copy = 10 p = 25 -- value = 25
section.p: With an array pointee, a subscript selects the element. Constant and runtime indices are both allowed:
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE arr[4] VAR POINTER ap AS VAR BYTE[4]
ap IS arr ap[0] = 50 -- arr[0] = 50 copy = ap[i] -- read element i
section.note: Plain assignment between two pointers is a store-through, not a pointer copy: q = p reads the value p points at and writes it through q. Use q IS p to copy the pointer itself.

section.title: Read-only pointees
section.p: A pointee declared CONST may be read through the pointer but not written. Binding it to a constant array is the usual way to walk a ROM lookup table:
section.codeblock:
CONST BYTE table[3] = {10, 20, 30} VAR POINTER cp AS CONST BYTE[3]
cp IS table copy = cp[1] -- 20

section.title: Pseudo-variables
section.p: A pointer may be bound to a pseudo-variable, in which case reads and writes go through its accessors: a read uses the 'get routine and a write uses the 'put routine. An indexed read of an array-shaped pseudo-variable (p[i]) uses its indexed accessor.
section.codeblock:
FUNCTION sensor'GET() RETURN BYTE IS ... END FUNCTION PROCEDURE sensor'PUT(BYTE IN value) IS ... END PROCEDURE
VAR POINTER p AS VAR BYTE p IS sensor copy = p -- calls sensor'GET p = 5 -- calls sensor'PUT
section.p: Pseudo-variable bindings live on scalar pointer variables. They cannot be stored in pointer-slot array elements or record members, and a pointer bound to a pseudo-variable cannot be copied with q = p (the store-through form drops the accessor link); read the value into an ordinary variable first. A pseudo-variable binding is also not carried through procedure parameters: a pointer formal receives the address only.

section.title: Pointers to dynamic strings
section.p: A pointer whose pointee contract is VAR STRING points at a dynamic string. Assignment and concatenation through the pointer act on the string it refers to:
section.codeblock:
CONST WORD _string_heap_size = 128 INCLUDE strings_dynamic VAR STRING text VAR POINTER p AS VAR STRING
p IS text p = "abc" p = p & "XY"

section.title: Pointer slots and WHEREIS
section.p: An array of pointers holds several bindings. Elements are bound with the same IS statement, including at runtime indices, and read and written through the element:
section.codeblock:
VAR BYTE a = 0 VAR BYTE b = 0 VAR BYTE value VAR POINTER slots[2] AS VAR BYTE
slots[0] IS a slots[1] IS b value = slots[1] -- 0 slots[k] IS b -- rebind slot k at run time
section.p: WHEREIS returns the address a pointer targets, or zero when the pointer is unbound. It accepts a pointer variable or an indexed slot:
section.codeblock: VAR DWORD addr addr = WHEREIS(slots[0]) addr = WHEREIS(a)

section.title: Checks
section.p: The compiler tracks whether each pointer has been bound and rejects reads, writes, subscripts, and self-binds of an unbound pointer. A pointer slot that has never been bound contains zero; indirect access through such a slot is refused at run time instead of reading address zero.
